title: DFS on New York (SoHo) ⚡
description: Visualizing DFS pathfinding on New York (SoHo)
ig_caption:
Depth First Search (DFS) Traversal on Real Street Maps—what happens when DFS explores city intersections first, not the shortest route? ⚡

In this visualization, each street intersection is a node and every connecting road segment is an edge. DFS uses a LIFO stack: it keeps going “deeper” down one path until it can’t, then backtracks—so the traversal order is highly sensitive to neighbor ordering (e.g., North→East→South→West).

✅ Breakdown (how to think like the algorithm):
• Pick a start intersection (start node)
• Visit as deep as possible along one branch
• Backtrack only when a dead end is reached
• Track visited nodes to avoid loops

Takeaway: DFS is amazing for exploring reachability and structure, but it’s not guaranteed to find the shortest path—use it strategically.

Debate question: If you wanted the fastest route across the city, would you still trust DFS, or switch to BFS/Dijkstra? 👇
